title: The mountain (Exodus 19–20)
hookLine: thunder, a shofar, the whole people at the foot of Sinai; the rabbis say every Jewish soul was there
tomorrow: the calf and the second tablets

cards: A huge crowd going quiet at once. A stadium during a moment of silence. A candlelight vigil.
Tens of thousands of people, and you can hear a coat rustle. Three months after leaving Egypt, the people camp at the foot of a mountain in the desert.
For three days they get ready: they wash their clothes, they wait, and a boundary is set around the mountain. On the third morning, the sky breaks open.

teach.b: Thunder. Lightning. A thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of a shofar, a ram's horn, growing louder.
The mountain smokes like a furnace, and it shakes. The whole people trembles.
Then God speaks the words Jews call aseret hadibrot, the Ten Words, which English calls the Ten Commandments. I am the LORD thy God, who brought you out of Egypt. Have no other gods.
Remember the Sabbath. Honor your father and mother. Do not murder, steal, lie, or covet.

Then comes a line that has puzzled readers ever since. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And all the people perceived the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the voice of the horn."
In Hebrew, the verb is ro'im, they saw.
They saw the voices. The rabbis took it literally: at Sinai, people saw what is usually heard. A midrash adds that when God spoke, no bird sang, no ox lowed, the sea didn't stir.
The whole world went silent to listen. Then a teaching you first met on day ten: who was there?
The Torah later says the covenant was made not only with those standing there that day, but also with those who were not there.
The rabbis read that to mean every Jewish soul, every future generation, and every person who would one day choose to become Jewish, stood at the foot of the mountain.
That's why many Jews tell the story in the first person: we stood at Sinai. It isn't a memory of ancestors. It's a place you were.

teach.h: ALL THAT THE LORD HATH SPOKEN WILL WE DO.
teach.b: And the people's answer, a few chapters later, became well-known too: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey."

how: Jews celebrate the giving of the Torah on Shavuot, seven weeks after Passover, when the Ten Commandments are read aloud in synagogue and many stay up all night studying.

Sinai, where the people heard the Ten Words

games.q: what's inside the mountain — tap the pairs.

s: in Hebrew they're called the Ten Commandments
the Hebrew name is aseret hadibrot, the Ten Words or Ten Sayings.
the verse says the people saw the thunder
they perceived, literally saw, the voices: the rabbis read it as seeing what is heard.
the rabbis taught only that generation stood at Sinai
they taught that every Jewish soul, even future converts, was there.

games.q: you're at the foot of the mountain. thunder, smoke, the shofar getting louder. the people are asked to accept the covenant. what do they say?
o: let us think about it first.
we will do, and we will listen.
games.why: "all that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey": in Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma, we will do and we will hear, doing first.

practice: The midrash says the whole world went still at Sinai, so try a small version for a minute: let the sounds around you come in, a fridge, a car, a bird, your own breath, without naming them.
Then, underneath them, listen for the quiet. If you pray, you might listen for what the quiet is saying; if you don't, just rest in it.

wordCard.voice: The mountain. Sinai, where the people stood in thunder and silence and heard the Ten Words, and where, the rabbis say, every soul was present.

orig.note: Hebrew: Mount Sinai. the Torah also calls it Horeb.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone was there. Whoever you meet stood at that mountain too, the old idea says. Day ninety-four, done.
